mathgap.title: Direct count assignment
mathgap.principle: When a statement explicitly gives a count for a person, set that person's current count to the given number.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence states "X has N items" (or a synonymous phrasing).
mathgap.example: Leaving a direct count statement unused or treating it as optional, resulting in an undefined variable.

mathgap.title: Directionality of more/fewer
mathgap.principle: Interpret "X has N more than Y" as X = Y + N, and "X has N fewer than Y" as X = Y - N, preserving the order of the names.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a comparative statement using "more" or "fewer" appears.
mathgap.example: Swapping the direction and writing Y = X + N for "X has N more than Y".

mathgap.title: Split‑all handling
mathgap.principle: If a person splits all of their items equally between two recipients, each recipient receives half of the giver's current count and the giver ends with zero.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement explicitly says a person splits all of their items equally between two others.
mathgap.example: Treating a split‑all as a fixed transfer of a known number instead of half of the giver's current amount.

mathgap.title: Sequential transfer handling
mathgap.principle: For a transfer "X gives N items to Y", subtract N from X's current count and add N to Y's current count, respecting the order of statements.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a transfer statement appears in the narrative.
mathgap.example: Applying a later transfer before an earlier one, causing the intermediate counts to be wrong.

mathgap.title: Signed‑difference substitution
mathgap.principle: If a signed difference (X − Y) appears in an equation and its numeric value is already known, replace the expression with that number to simplify the equation.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When you have computed X − Y from known counts and it appears on either side of an equality.
mathgap.example: Leaving a known (X − Y) as a symbolic term instead of substituting its numeric value, leaving the system unsimplified.

mathgap.title: Chronological evaluation
mathgap.principle: Process statements in the exact order they appear; later statements refer to counts after earlier transfers and updates have been applied.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For any problem containing transfers, comparisons, or updates that depend on previous information.
mathgap.example: Evaluating a comparison before processing a prior transfer that changes the involved counts, leading to an incorrect relationship.

mathgap.title: Conditional transfer handling
mathgap.principle: For a transfer that is conditional on a count, first evaluate the condition using the current counts before applying the transfer.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement includes a condition such as "If X has at least N, then X gives ...".
mathgap.example: Applying a conditional transfer without checking the condition, resulting in an impossible negative count.

mathgap.title: Target variable dependency analysis
mathgap.principle: Identify which equations and variables directly or indirectly affect the queried person, and ignore statements that do not influence that variable.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains many unrelated statements or a large system of equations.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire system of equations, including irrelevant variables, which wastes effort and can cause confusion.

mathgap.title: Signed difference equality parsing
mathgap.principle: Parse statements of the form "The number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of X that C and D have" as a signed difference equation (A − B) = (C − D), preserving the order of the names.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a sentence mentions both a "more than" comparison and a "difference between" two other persons.
mathgap.example: Interpreting the phrase as an absolute difference or swapping the order of terms, e.g., treating (A − B) = (C − D) as |A − B| = |C − D|.

mathgap.title: Solve signed difference equations with unknowns
mathgap.principle: When a signed difference equality (A − B) = (C − D) contains unknown variables, rearrange it into a linear form (e.g., A = B + C − D) and use substitution with other equations to solve for the unknowns.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever you encounter a signed difference equality where not all four variables have known numeric values.
mathgap.example: Assuming (A − B) = (C − D) implies A = C and B = D, which is incorrect because the equality relates differences, not individual values.

mathgap.description: Treating signed difference statements as absolute differences or swapping term order
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model confuses the phrasing of signed differences with absolute differences, losing sign information and potentially reversing terms.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Parse signed difference statements as ordered expressions (A − B) and preserve the order when forming equations.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model processes transfers out of order, assuming they are independent of earlier updates.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Apply each transfer in the exact order it appears, updating counts after each step before evaluating later statements.

mathgap.description: Assuming explicit counts are final after all transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats direct count assignments as immutable, forgetting that later transfers can modify those counts.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat a direct count as the current count at that point; allow subsequent statements (including transfers) to modify it.

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model overlooks the condition part of a conditional transfer and applies the transfer unconditionally.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Evaluate the condition using the current counts before applying the transfer; only execute the transfer if the condition holds.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting multiplicative increase statements as additive
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model reads phrases like "twice as many" as "adds a fixed amount" instead of multiplying.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Recognize multiplicative language (e.g., "twice", "double", "three times") and apply the appropriate multiplication to the count.
